title: Serving 2 Million Models Without Melting: Scaling the Hugging Face Hub — Arek Borucki, Hugging Face

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 94%).

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: Hugging Face Hub is the canonical developer platform for ML models and datasets. The talk is about scaling this platform's infrastructure.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The infrastructure patterns (MongoDB sharding, Kubernetes autoscaling, Lucene search) are general-purpose and applicable beyond AI, but the talk is framed in the context of serving AI model artifacts to AI engineers.

summary: Arek Borucki, ML Platform & Database Engineer at Hugging Face, presents the infrastructure scaling journey of the Hugging Face Hub, which serves 14 million users, 3 million public models, 1 million datasets, and 50,000 organizations including 30% of the Fortune 500. The talk covers how the Hub grew from 20,000 to 3 million models (~150x increase), making search the hardest scaling problem since even 1% of 14 million users experiencing slow search means 140,000 affected people, making P99 latency the critical metric. The architecture separates metadata (stored in MongoDB Atlas), model artifacts (stored in S3), and compute (Kubernetes), enabling each layer to scale independently. Model names are pre-tokenized at insert time into arrays in a denormalized read-only collection. The old regex-based search on these token arrays did not scale, so the team migrated to Atlas Search, which uses Apache Lucene via a mongot process and is queried through MongoDB's $search aggregation operator with autocomplete, ranked by a trending score recalculated every five minutes from seven days of downloads and likes. The database runs on a seven-node MongoDB cluster with a single primary for writes, reads distributed across secondaries, and a hidden analytics node invisible to the application for heavy reporting. Query routing ensures the primary handles only strong-consistency operations while complex aggregations and ad hoc queries go to secondaries or the hidden node. As growth continues, sharding is the next step, splitting data across shards each with their own replica sets. On the Kubernetes side, the Hub scales from 10 to 500 pods via HPA, with CastAI handling node-level autoscaling when pods are pending due to capacity constraints. The team is migrating from HPA to KEDA, which scales on real application metrics like requests per second and event loop utilization, detecting cases where CPU is low but request queues are high.
whyItMatters: These concepts form a cohesive story about scaling AI platform infrastructure at internet scale. The separation of concerns (metadata in MongoDB, artifacts in S3, compute on Kubernetes) is the architectural foundation that enables each layer to scale independently. Within that foundation, pre-tokenization and Atlas Search solve the search scalability problem specific to AI model registries where millions of models must be discoverable by name. The hidden analytics node and query routing protect the primary database from analytical workload interference. P99 latency thinking provides the quantitative motivation: at 14M users, tail latency directly impacts hundreds of thousands of people. KEDA and CastAI handle the compute layer's elastic scaling, with KEDA specifically addressing the I/O-bound nature of request-driven AI platform workloads. Sharding represents the next frontier for the database layer. Together, these concepts illustrate that operating a platform serving the global AI community requires combining database engineering (Atlas Search, query routing, sharding), cloud-native orchestration (HPA, KEDA, CastAI), and AI-specific design decisions (artifact separation, community-driven ranking) into a unified scaling strategy. The talk demonstrates that no single technology solves the problem; it is the composition of these patterns that enables the Hub to serve 3 million models to 14 million users.
temporalContext: Video published July 28, 2026. Research conducted as of August 22, 2026. The talk was presented at a MongoDB community event (MongoDB Local London per secondary sources). The Hugging Face Hub incident post-mortem from May 2024 corroborates the MongoDB Atlas infrastructure described. KEDA graduated from CNCF on August 22, 2023. The mongot source-available announcement was January 2026. The MongoDB Atlas Search product page was last updated January 2025. Datasets grew from 10K in 2022 to 1 million by the time of the talk, illustrating the rapid scaling trajectory.

concepts.name: Hugging Face Hub as AI model registry platform
concepts.explanation: The Hugging Face Hub is the canonical platform for hosting and discovering ML models, datasets, and applications, serving 3 million public models, 1 million datasets, and 50,000 organizations for over 14 million users including 30% of Fortune 500. First-party Hugging Face documentation and engineering blog confirm the Hub's role as the primary ML model distribution platform.
concepts.importance: The Hub is the central infrastructure that the global ML community depends on for model distribution and discovery; understanding its scaling challenges provides essential insight into operating AI platforms at internet scale.

concepts.name: Model artifact storage (tokenizers, weights, configs in S3)
concepts.explanation: Model artifacts including tokenizer files, weight files, and configuration files are stored in S3 rather than in the metadata database, enabling independent scaling of binary storage from metadata and compute. This separates potentially gigabyte-scale AI model binaries from lightweight metadata records.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates the pattern of separating AI model binaries from metadata records, a critical design decision for any model registry dealing with large model files that grow with model parameter counts.

concepts.name: AI model discovery via community-driven trending signals
concepts.explanation: Search results are ranked by a trending score derived from downloads and likes over seven days, recalculated every five minutes. This provides a community-driven relevance signal for model discovery that goes beyond simple text matching, reflecting the AI community's adoption velocity for models.
concepts.importance: Shows how AI model discovery requires specialized ranking signals (community engagement and adoption metrics) distinct from traditional web search ranking, reflecting the unique dynamics of the ML model ecosystem.

concepts.name: MongoDB Atlas Search via mongot (Apache Lucene)
concepts.explanation: MongoDB Atlas Search uses a separate process called mongot that wraps Apache Lucene to provide full-text search capabilities. The $search aggregation pipeline operator queries Atlas Search indexes, replacing regex-based queries that failed to scale at Hugging Face's 3 million model catalog. First-party MongoDB documentation and engineering blog confirm mongot wraps Lucene, mongod proxies $search queries to mongot, and Atlas Search alleviates $regex limitations.
concepts.importance: Core architectural decision that resolved search latency at scale; demonstrates the pattern of integrating a specialized search engine within a document database via a sidecar process.

concepts.name: Pre-tokenization at insert time into denormalized read collections
concepts.explanation: Model names are tokenized into arrays at document insert time (e.g., meta-llama/llama-3.1-8b becomes ['meta', 'llama', '3.1', '8b']) and stored in a denormalized read-only MongoDB collection, avoiding query-time tokenization overhead and enabling fast autocomplete search.
concepts.importance: Key optimization pattern for high-throughput autocomplete search; separates write-time complexity from read-time performance and is a transferable technique for any catalog search system.

concepts.name: MongoDB replica set query routing with hidden analytics node
concepts.explanation: The seven-node MongoDB cluster uses a single primary for all writes, distributes reads across secondaries, and includes a hidden analytics node invisible to the application and MongoDB driver for heavy reporting and ad hoc queries. Strong-consistency operations stay on primary; complex aggregations, change streams, and ad hoc queries go to secondaries or the hidden node.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates production-grade read isolation patterns that protect the primary from analytical workload interference, critical for maintaining write performance at 14M-user scale.

concepts.name: Database sharding (replica set to sharded cluster progression)
concepts.explanation: When a single replica set becomes insufficient, sharding splits data across shards each with their own primary and secondaries. Unlike a replica set where each node holds the full dataset, sharded clusters hold only part per shard, scaling CPU, memory, storage, reads, and writes horizontally. The MongoDB balancer distributes data across shards. Shard key selection is called out as non-trivial.
concepts.importance: The next scaling step for Hugging Face's database; represents the industry-standard horizontal scaling path for document databases at massive data volume.

concepts.name: KEDA event-driven autoscaling replacing HPA
concepts.explanation: KEDA replaces Kubernetes HPA to scale pods based on real application metrics like requests per second and event loop utilization rather than just CPU and memory. This catches cases where CPU is low but the request queue is high, which HPA cannot detect. KEDA is a CNCF graduated project confirmed by first-party sources.
concepts.importance: Addresses the blind spot of CPU/memory-based autoscaling for I/O-bound workloads; a pattern validated by multiple organizations including Zapier and relevant to any request-driven microservice.

concepts.name: Two-level Kubernetes autoscaling (HPA pods + CastAI nodes)
concepts.explanation: The Hub scales from 10 to 500 pods via HPA based on CPU and memory thresholds. CastAI handles node-level autoscaling by detecting unschedulable pods and dynamically provisioning right-sized nodes when capacity constraints prevent pod scheduling. First-party CastAI documentation confirms this autoscaler behavior.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates the two-level autoscaling pattern (pod-level via HPA, node-level via CastAI) needed for elastic cloud-native infrastructure where both pod count and underlying compute capacity must scale.

concepts.name: P99 latency-first scaling mindset
concepts.explanation: At 14 million users, even 1% experiencing slow search means 140,000 affected people, making P99 latency the critical metric over P50. This drives investments in pre-tokenization, Atlas Search, query routing, and autoscaling. At 20,000 models any query is fast even without an index; at 3 million the same approach breaks.
concepts.importance: Provides the quantitative justification for infrastructure investments at massive scale; a key principle for any platform serving millions of users where tail latency dominates user experience.

concepts.name: Separation of concerns: metadata vs artifacts vs compute
concepts.explanation: MongoDB Atlas stores all metadata (users, repos, models, datasets, billing, access control), S3 stores model artifacts (tokenizers, weights, configs), and Kubernetes handles compute. This separation allows each layer to scale independently according to its own demand profile.
concepts.importance: Foundational architectural principle enabling independent scaling of the three major system dimensions; a transferable pattern for any large-scale platform architecture.

concepts.name: Trending score ranking pipeline
concepts.explanation: Search results are ranked by a trending score calculated from downloads and likes over the last seven days, recalculated every five minutes. This ranking pipeline runs as part of the $search aggregation, sorting model results by community engagement metrics.
concepts.importance: Shows how to combine full-text search with custom relevance signals in an aggregation pipeline; demonstrates the pattern of periodically recomputing ranking scores for near-real-time relevance.

sections.title: Introduction and Scale
sections.summary: Arek Borucki introduces himself as an ML platform and database engineer at Hugging Face. The Hub serves 14 million users, 3 million public models, 1 million datasets, 50,000 organizations, and 30% of Fortune 500. Growth from 20,000 to 3 million models is a 150x increase. Datasets grew from 10K in 2022 to 1 million today.

sections.title: Why Search at Scale Is Hard
sections.summary: At 20,000 models any query is fast even without an index. At 3 million the same approach breaks. Even 1% of 14 million users hitting slow search means 140,000 affected users. P99 is more important than P50, driving investments in pre-tokenization, denormalized read collections, MongoDB full-text search via Apache Lucene, Kubernetes autoscaling, and upcoming database sharding.

sections.title: High-Level Architecture and Request Flow
sections.summary: Requests flow from frontend to the Hub API running on Kubernetes with horizontal pod autoscaler, then to MongoDB Atlas as the source of truth for metadata. MongoDB stores all metadata (users, repos, models, datasets, billing, access control) while model artifacts (tokenizers, weights, configs) are stored in S3. This separation allows metadata, binary storage, and compute to scale independently.

sections.title: How Search Works: The Llama Example
sections.summary: Searching for 'llama' hits a denormalized read-only collection. Model names are pre-tokenized at insert time into arrays (e.g., meta-llama/llama-3.1-8b becomes tokens like meta, llama, 3.1, 8b). A findOne query demonstrates the searchTokens array stored in each document.

sections.title: From Regex to Atlas Search Ranking
sections.summary: The old approach used MongoDB find with $regex on searchTokens sorted by trending score (downloads and likes over seven days, recalculated every five minutes). Regex did not scale, causing latency issues. They switched to Atlas Search using Apache Lucene via a mongot process, queried with the $search operator in an aggregation pipeline with autocomplete, still sorted by trending score, which resolved latency problems.

sections.title: Seven-Node MongoDB Cluster and Query Routing
sections.summary: The seven-node cluster has one primary for all writes and distributed reads across secondaries. A hidden analytics node replicates from primary but is invisible to the application and MongoDB driver, used for heavy reporting and ad hoc queries. Query routing: strong-consistency queries stay on primary; complex aggregations, change streams, and ad hoc queries go to secondaries or the hidden node. The principle is primary focuses only on what it must do.

sections.title: Sharding the Database
sections.summary: At continued growth a single replica set will not suffice. Sharding splits data across shards, each with its own primary and secondaries. Replica sets hold the full dataset on each node; sharded clusters hold only part per shard. The MongoDB balancer distributes data across shards. Sharding scales CPU, memory, storage, reads, and writes. Shard key selection is non-trivial.

sections.title: Kubernetes Autoscaling: HPA, CastAI, and KEDA
sections.summary: The Hub runs on Kubernetes with HPA scaling 10 to 500 pods based on CPU and memory thresholds. CastAI handles node-level autoscaling when pods are pending due to capacity constraints. They are migrating from HPA to KEDA, which scales on real application metrics like requests per second and event loop utilization, detecting cases where CPU is low but request queue is high. The goal is seamless scaling invisible to users.

demonstrations: Shows a MongoDB findOne query projecting the searchTokens array for model meta-llama/llama-3.1-8b, demonstrating pre-tokenized tokens like 'meta', 'llama', '3.1', '8b' stored in the document

Shows the old regex-based search query using find with $regex on searchTokens sorted by trending score, contrasted with the new Atlas Search query using $search with autocomplete on the model_search index, also sorted by trending score

organization.name: Hugging Face
organization.summary: Hugging Face is an independent company founded in 2016, headquartered in Paris, France with US operations. It operates the Hugging Face Hub, the world's largest open-source AI model repository serving 14M+ users, 3M+ models, 1M+ datasets, and 50,000+ organizations including 30% of the Fortune 500. The company has 200-300 employees distributed across 41 countries and raised $100M in Series C funding led by Lux Capital. The Hub's infrastructure uses MongoDB Atlas for metadata, S3 for model artifacts, and Kubernetes for compute with HPA/KEDA autoscaling.
organization.status: Active and operating. The Hub continues to grow with 3M+ models, 1M+ datasets, 14M+ users, and 50,000+ organizations. Hugging Face has active hiring and ongoing infrastructure scaling efforts including migration to KEDA and plans for MongoDB sharding.

technologies.label: MongoDB Atlas Search via mongot and Apache Lucene
technologies.summary: MongoDB Atlas Search is the core search technology powering model discovery on the Hugging Face Hub. It replaced a regex-based approach on pre-tokenized search token arrays that failed to scale at 3 million models. Atlas Search uses Apache Lucene via a separate process called mongot, queried through MongoDB's $search aggregation pipeline operator with autocomplete support. Model names are pre-tokenized at insert time into arrays stored in a denormalized read-only collection, avoiding query-time tokenization overhead. Search results are ranked by a trending score derived from downloads and likes over seven days, recalculated every five minutes. First-party MongoDB documentation, product pages, and the mongot source-available blog post (January 2026) confirm all architectural claims. A first-party Hugging Face engineering blog independently corroborates the Hub's MongoDB Atlas usage in production.
technologies.role: Central technology story: the talk's primary narrative is the migration from regex-based search to Atlas Search (Apache Lucene via mongot) to resolve P99 latency at 3M model scale, with pre-tokenization and trending score ranking as supporting techniques.

technologies.label: MongoDB cluster architecture: replica set, hidden analytics node, and sharding progression
technologies.summary: The Hugging Face Hub runs on a seven-node MongoDB Atlas replica set with a single primary handling all writes, reads distributed across secondaries, and a hidden analytics node invisible to the application and MongoDB driver for heavy reporting and ad hoc queries. The query routing principle keeps the primary focused on strong-consistency operations while pushing complex aggregations, change streams, and ad hoc queries to secondaries or the hidden node. As growth continues, sharding is the next step: splitting data across shards each with their own primary and secondaries, with the MongoDB balancer distributing data. Shard key selection is called out as non-trivial. A first-party Hugging Face incident post-mortem (May 2024) independently corroborates MongoDB Atlas usage with cluster autoscaling in production.
technologies.role: Second major technology story: after search, the talk covers the database cluster architecture (seven nodes, hidden analytics node, query routing) and the future scaling path (sharding) when the replica set reaches its limits.

technologies.label: Kubernetes autoscaling: HPA, KEDA, and CastAI
technologies.primary: Kubernetes autoscaling (HPA to KEDA migration with CastAI node provisioning)
technologies.summary: The Hugging Face Hub runs on Kubernetes with a two-level autoscaling architecture. At the pod level, HPA scales from 10 to 500 pods based on CPU and memory thresholds. CastAI handles node-level autoscaling by detecting unschedulable pods and dynamically provisioning right-sized nodes when capacity constraints prevent scheduling. The team is migrating from HPA to KEDA, a CNCF graduated project (August 22, 2023) that scales on real application metrics like requests per second and event loop utilization, detecting cases where CPU is low but request queues are high. KEDA extends HPA with external metrics via Prometheus rather than replacing it entirely. First-party KEDA homepage, CNCF project page, and graduation press release confirm its status. CastAI first-party homepage and autoscaler documentation confirm node-level provisioning behavior. Secondary sources (Kedify, Nearform, Zapier) corroborate that KEDA's event-driven scaling catches I/O-bound workloads that CPU-based HPA misses.
technologies.role: Third major technology story: the Kubernetes compute layer scaling from 10 to 500 pods with HPA, CastAI for node provisioning, and the migration to KEDA for event-loop-utilization-based scaling.

technologies.label: Hugging Face Hub separation of concerns: metadata, artifacts, and compute
technologies.primary: Separation of concerns architecture (metadata in MongoDB, artifacts in S3, compute on Kubernetes)
technologies.summary: The Hugging Face Hub's foundational architectural principle is the separation of concerns across three layers: MongoDB Atlas stores all metadata (users, repositories, models, datasets, billing, access control), Amazon S3 stores model artifacts (tokenizer files, weight files, configuration files), and Kubernetes handles compute (the Hub API with horizontal pod autoscaling). This separation allows each layer to scale independently according to its own demand profile. Within MongoDB, a denormalized read-only collection stores pre-tokenized model names for search, further separating read-optimized search data from write-heavy source-of-truth collections. At 14 million users with 3 million models, even 1% experiencing slow search means 140,000 affected people, making P99 latency the critical metric that drives all architectural decisions. First-party Hugging Face documentation and engineering blog corroborate the platform's infrastructure.
technologies.role: Foundational architecture: the separation of metadata, artifacts, and compute is the overarching design principle that contextualizes all other technology families discussed in the talk.
